title: Engineering Practices
summary: Testing, performance, async code, secure coding and system design: the habits that turn working code into production code.

lessons.title: Automated testing and TDD

concept.text:
A test is a small piece of code that runs your code and checks the result. Once written, it runs in seconds, every time, so you find out the moment a change breaks something instead of hearing it from a user.

Most tests follow **arrange, act, assert**: set up the input, call the code, check the output. Good test suites are shaped like a pyramid: many fast **unit tests** for single functions, fewer **integration tests** for parts working together, and a handful of slow **end-to-end tests** that drive the real app.

**Test-driven development (TDD)** flips the order: write a failing test first, write just enough code to pass it, then tidy up. The failing test proves the test can actually catch the bug.
concept.analogy: Tests are a smoke detector for your code. You install it once, and from then on it watches every change you make, so a small fire gets noticed before it spreads.

visual.caption: The testing pyramid: lots of fast tests at the bottom, a few slow ones at the top.

layers.name: End-to-end tests
layers.detail: Drive the real app like a user. Slow and fragile, so keep them few.

layers.name: Integration tests
layers.detail: Check that parts work together: your code plus a real database or API.

layers.name: Unit tests
layers.detail: One function at a time, in milliseconds. Most of your tests live here.

steps.title: Arrange, act, assert
steps.text: Every test sets up an input, calls the code, and asserts what should come back. `assert` stops with an error if the condition is false.
steps.code:
def test_total():
    cart = [10, 5, 5]          # arrange
    result = sum(cart)         # act
    assert result == 20        # assert

steps.title: Test the edges, not just the happy path
steps.text: Bugs hide at the boundaries: empty input, one item, huge numbers, odd characters, missing values. Write a test for each edge you can think of.

steps.title: Red, green, refactor
steps.text: In TDD you write the test first and watch it fail (red), write the simplest code that passes (green), then clean the code up while the test keeps you safe (refactor).

steps.title: Run them automatically
steps.text: Real projects use a test runner such as `pytest` (Python) or `vitest` (JavaScript), and a CI service runs every test on every push. A red build blocks the merge.
steps.code:
# Python, from the terminal
pip install pytest
pytest          # finds and runs every test_*.py file

challenge.prompt: One test fails because `slugify` keeps punctuation. Fix the function so all three tests pass, then add a fourth test proving an empty title gives an empty slug.
challenge.hint: `re.findall(r"[a-z0-9]+", text)` returns only the runs of letters and digits. Remove apostrophes first so "What's" becomes "whats".

takeaways: A test runs your code and checks the result automatically, in seconds.
Write many fast unit tests, fewer integration tests and only a few end-to-end tests.
Test the edges: empty, single, huge and unusual inputs.
In TDD, a test that fails first proves it can catch the bug.

lessons.title: Performance and Big-O

concept.text:
Code that is instant on 100 items can freeze on a million. **Big-O notation** describes how the work grows as the input grows, ignoring the details that do not matter at scale.

**O(1)** stays flat no matter the size. **O(n)** grows in step with the input. **O(n²)** squares it: double the input, four times the work. That last one usually comes from a loop inside a loop.

The biggest speed-ups rarely come from clever tricks. They come from choosing the right data structure, like a set or dictionary instead of a list when you need to look things up.
concept.analogy: Finding a friend at a concert: walking past every seat is O(n). Calling their phone is O(1), no matter how big the crowd. Asking every person to compare tickets with every other person is O(n²), and the concert ends before you finish.

visual.caption: Roughly how many steps each growth rate needs.
rows: Look up a key in a dictionary or set

steps.title: Count how the work grows
steps.text: Ask: if the input doubles, what happens to the work? One loop over the data doubles it, O(n). A loop inside a loop over the same data quadruples it, O(n²).

steps.title: Know your data structures
steps.text: `x in my_list` checks items one by one, O(n). `x in my_set` and `my_dict[key]` jump straight to the answer using a hash, O(1) on average.
steps.code:
emails = ["a@x.com", "b@x.com"]        # in: O(n)
email_set = set(emails)                # in: O(1)
print("b@x.com" in email_set)

steps.title: Trade memory for speed
steps.text: Building a set or a lookup dictionary costs extra memory once, then makes every later lookup instant. That is usually a great deal.

steps.title: Measure before you optimise
steps.text: Guesses about speed are often wrong. Time the real code (`time.perf_counter()`, or a profiler) and fix the slowest part first. A clear O(n) solution beats a clever one nobody can read.

interactive.starter:
import time

n = 20000
items = list(range(n))
lookups = list(range(0, n, 7))

start = time.perf_counter()
found = sum(1 for x in lookups if x in items)   # list: checks items one by one
list_time = time.perf_counter() - start

as_set = set(items)
start = time.perf_counter()
found = sum(1 for x in lookups if x in as_set)  # set: jumps straight to the answer
set_time = max(time.perf_counter() - start, 1e-6)

print(f"{len(lookups)} lookups in {n} items")
print(f"list: {list_time * 1000:.1f} ms")
print(f"set:  {set_time * 1000:.2f} ms")
print(f"the set was about {list_time / set_time:.0f}x faster")

challenge.prompt: `has_duplicates` compares every pair of items, which is O(n²). Rewrite it to be O(n) and compare the timing.
challenge.hint: Walk through the list once, remembering what you have already seen in a set. If an item is already in the set, you found a duplicate.
challenge.solution:
import time

def has_duplicates(items):
    seen = set()
    for item in items:
        if item in seen:
            return True
        seen.add(item)
    return False

print(has_duplicates([3, 1, 4, 1, 5]))
start = time.perf_counter()
print(has_duplicates(list(range(3000))))
print(f"{(time.perf_counter() - start) * 1000:.1f} ms")

takeaways: Big-O describes how work grows with input size, not exact speed.
A loop inside a loop over the same data is O(n²) and gets slow fast.
Sets and dictionaries look things up in O(1) on average. Lists take O(n).
Measure first, then fix the slowest part.

lessons.title: Async code: promises and concurrency

concept.text:
Most of the time a program spends "working" it is actually waiting: for a network response, a database or a file. **Asynchronous** code lets it start a slow task, do other things while it waits, and pick the result up when it is ready.

In JavaScript a slow operation returns a **promise**: a placeholder for a value that will arrive later. `await` pauses the current function until the promise settles, without freezing the rest of the program.

The common mistake is awaiting independent tasks one after another. If three requests do not depend on each other, start them together with `Promise.all` and the total wait becomes the longest one, not the sum. That is **concurrency**: many tasks in progress at once, even on a single thread.
concept.analogy: A cook making dinner does not stand and watch the pasta boil. They put the water on, chop vegetables while it heats, and start the sauce meanwhile. One cook, several dishes in progress: that is concurrency.

visual.caption: With Promise.all, three requests overlap. The total time is the slowest one, not the sum.

steps.title: await pauses one function, not the program
steps.text: While a function waits on `await`, the event loop keeps running other code, timers and clicks. Nothing freezes.

steps.title: Start independent work together
steps.text: Call the functions first (each returns a promise immediately), then await them all at once.

steps.title: Decide what failure means
steps.text: `Promise.all` rejects as soon as one task fails. Use `Promise.allSettled` when you want every result, success or failure, and wrap awaits in `try` and `catch`.
steps.code:
const results = await Promise.allSettled([a(), b(), c()])
const failed = results.filter((r) => r.status === "rejected")

steps.title: Limit how much runs at once
steps.text: Firing 10,000 requests together can overload a server or hit rate limits. Real code caps concurrency, for example at 5 requests at a time.

steps.title: Watch for race conditions
steps.text: When two tasks read and update the same value while waiting, one can overwrite the other. Keep shared state small, and update it in one place.

challenge.prompt: Write `mapWithLimit(items, limit, fn)`: call `fn` on every item, never with more than `limit` calls running at once, and return the results in the original order. The starter runs all seven downloads at once; yours should report `most at once: 3`.
challenge.hint: Start `limit` "workers". Each worker loops: take the next unclaimed index, await `fn` for it, store the result at that index, repeat until no items are left. Await all the workers with `Promise.all`.

takeaways: A promise is a placeholder for a value that arrives later. await waits for it without freezing the program.
Start independent tasks together with Promise.all. The total time becomes the slowest task, not the sum.
Use Promise.allSettled when one failure should not discard the other results.
Cap concurrency for large batches, and keep shared state simple to avoid race conditions.

lessons.title: Secure coding: injection and the OWASP Top 10

concept.text:
Most real-world breaches do not involve genius hackers. They exploit a short list of everyday coding mistakes, which the **OWASP Top 10** tracks and ranks.

The classic one is **injection**: the program builds a command, such as an SQL query, by pasting user input straight into it. If the input contains SQL syntax, the attacker is now writing part of your query. The same idea drives **cross-site scripting (XSS)**, where input is pasted into a web page and runs as a script.

The fix is a habit, not a trick: **never mix untrusted data into code**. Use parameterised queries, escape output, check permissions on every request, and keep secrets out of your source code.
concept.analogy: Injection is like a bank teller who reads your deposit slip aloud as instructions. Write "deposit $10. Also, give me the contents of the vault" on the slip, and the teller just does it. A safe teller only ever reads the slip as an amount.

visual.caption: Six of the most common risks on the OWASP Top 10.

items.title: Broken access control
items.text: Users can reach data or actions they should not, for example by changing an ID in the URL.

items.title: Injection
items.text: Untrusted input is treated as code: SQL injection, command injection, XSS.

items.title: Cryptographic failures
items.text: Sensitive data sent or stored without strong encryption, or passwords hashed weakly.

items.title: Security misconfiguration
items.text: Default passwords, debug mode in production, missing security headers.

items.title: Vulnerable components
items.text: Outdated libraries with known flaws. Update dependencies and scan them.

items.title: Authentication failures
items.text: No rate limiting, weak passwords allowed, sessions that never expire.

steps.title: See the vulnerable pattern
steps.text: This login code pastes input straight into the query. Whatever the user types becomes part of the SQL.
steps.code:
# DON'T: string building
query = f"SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '{name}' AND password_hash = '{pw}'"
db.execute(query)

steps.title: Use parameterised queries
steps.text: Pass input separately with placeholders. The database treats it strictly as data, so quotes and SQL keywords lose their power.
steps.code:
# DO: placeholders
db.execute(
    "SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = ? AND password_hash = ?",
    (name, pw_hash),
)

steps.title: Escape output to stop XSS
steps.text: When showing user text in a page, insert it as text, never as HTML. Frameworks like React escape by default; avoid bypasses such as `innerHTML` and `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` with user data. A Content-Security-Policy header is a strong second layer.

steps.title: Check access on the server, every time
steps.text: Hiding a button is not security. Before returning or changing data, the server must check that this user owns it or has the right role.

steps.title: Keep secrets and dependencies clean
steps.text: API keys and passwords go in environment variables or a secrets manager, never in Git. Update dependencies regularly and let tools like Dependabot flag known vulnerabilities.

interactive.seed: CREATE TABLE users(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, password_hash TEXT, role TEXT); INSERT INTO users(name, password_hash, role) VALUES ('ava','$2b$12$Qx..a1','admin'),('ben','$2b$12$Wm..b2','member'),('cy','$2b$12$Lp..c3','member');
interactive.starter:
-- The login code builds its query by pasting in what the user typed:
--   "... WHERE name = '" + name + "' AND password_hash = '" + pw + "'"
-- An attacker types this into the name box:   ' OR '1'='1' --
-- This is the query the database receives. Run it.
SELECT id, name, role FROM users
WHERE name = '' OR '1'='1' --' AND password_hash = 'anything';

-- '1'='1' is always true, and -- turns the password check into a comment.
-- Now run a normal failed login for comparison:
-- SELECT id, name, role FROM users WHERE name = 'ben' AND password_hash = 'wrong';

challenge.prompt:
A public endpoint, `GET /invoice?id=42`, runs these three lines. List every security problem you can find, with a fix for each. `invoice_id = request.args["id"]` `row = db.execute(f"SELECT * FROM invoices WHERE id = {invoice_id}").fetchone()` `return f"

Invoice for {row['customer_name']}

"`
challenge.hint: Look at three things: how the query is built, whose invoice is returned, and how the customer name gets into the HTML.
challenge.solution:
1. **SQL injection.** `invoice_id` is pasted into the query. An attacker can send `1 OR 1=1` or worse. Fix: `db.execute("SELECT * FROM invoices WHERE id = ?", (invoice_id,))`.

2. **Broken access control.** Any visitor can read any invoice by changing the ID. Fix: require login and add `AND user_id = ?` with the signed-in user's ID, returning 404 if no row matches.

3. **XSS.** `customer_name` goes into HTML unescaped. A name like `<script>...</script>` would run in the viewer's browser. Fix: escape it (`html.escape(...)`) or render through a template engine that escapes by default.

4. **Missing error handling.** If no invoice matches, `row` is `None` and the code crashes, possibly leaking a stack trace. Fix: return a clean 404.

takeaways: Never paste untrusted input into SQL, shell commands or HTML. Keep data and code separate.
Parameterised queries stop SQL injection. Escaping output stops XSS.
Check permissions on the server for every request. Hidden buttons are not security.
Keep secrets out of Git and dependencies up to date.

lessons.title: System design: scaling a web app

concept.text:
One server and one database can carry a surprising amount of traffic. **System design** is about what to add, and in what order, when they cannot.

The usual moves: put a **load balancer** in front of several identical app servers; make those servers **stateless** so any of them can handle any request; add a **cache** so repeated reads skip the database; add **read replicas** when reads outgrow one database; push slow work onto a **queue** for background workers; and serve images and scripts from a **CDN** close to the user.

Every addition solves one bottleneck and brings new problems, such as stale cache data or more moving parts to monitor. Good design starts with measuring where the real bottleneck is.
concept.analogy: A food truck grows into a restaurant. You hire more cooks (app servers), a host to seat guests evenly (load balancer), prep popular dishes in advance (cache), and send catering orders to a back kitchen (queue) so walk-in customers are not kept waiting.

visual.caption: A common shape for a web app that has outgrown one server.

nodes.label: CDN
nodes.detail: Serves images, CSS and JS from nearby

nodes.label: App servers
nodes.detail: Identical and stateless. Add more as needed

nodes.label: Database
nodes.detail: One primary for writes, replicas for reads

nodes.label: Queue + workers
nodes.detail: Emails, video encoding and reports run in the background

steps.title: Measure the bottleneck
steps.text: Is it CPU on the app servers, slow database queries, or one heavy endpoint? Add an index or fix one query before buying more servers.

steps.title: Make app servers stateless
steps.text: Store sessions and uploads in a shared database, cache or object storage, not in one server's memory or disk. Then any server can take any request, and you can add or remove servers freely.

steps.title: Cache what is read often
steps.text: With **cache-aside**, the app checks the cache first and only queries the database on a miss, then stores the result with an expiry time. The hard part is invalidation: deciding when cached data is out of date.
steps.code:
value = cache.get(key)
if value is None:
    value = db.query(...)
    cache.set(key, value, ttl=300)  # expires after 5 minutes

steps.title: Move slow work to a queue
steps.text: If a request triggers something slow, like sending email or resizing images, put a job on a queue and respond immediately. Background workers process jobs at their own pace and can retry failures.

steps.title: Scale the database last and carefully
steps.text: Read replicas handle more reads but may lag a moment behind the primary. Splitting data across several databases (**sharding**) handles more writes but makes queries and transactions much harder.

questions.q: Users get logged out at random after you add a second app server. What is the most likely cause?
options: The load balancer is too slow
Sessions are stored in each server's memory
The CDN is caching the login page
questions.explain: Requests alternate between servers, and the second server has never seen the session. Store sessions somewhere shared so the servers stay stateless.

questions.q: Your product page is read 10,000 times for every time it changes. What helps most?
options: A cache with a short expiry
questions.explain: Read-heavy, rarely changing data is the ideal case for caching. Most requests never touch the database.

questions.q: Sign-up takes 6 seconds because it waits for a welcome email to send. What is the best fix?
options: Put the email on a queue and respond right away
questions.explain: The user does not need to wait for the email. A background worker sends it, and can retry if the mail service is down.

questions.q: A user updates their profile, refreshes, and briefly sees the old version. Reads come from a replica. Why?
questions.explain: Replicas copy changes from the primary with a small delay. Read the user's own recent changes from the primary to avoid this.

challenge.prompt: A quiz app runs on one server with one database and has 500 users. A school district will roll it out to 200,000 students next month, all taking a quiz at 9:00 on Monday. Outline what you would change, in order, and why.
challenge.hint: Think about the shape of the traffic: a huge spike at one moment, mostly reading quiz questions, then a burst of answer submissions.
challenge.solution:
1. **Measure first.** Load-test the current app to find the first bottleneck, and fix slow queries and missing indexes.

2. **Static assets to a CDN**, so the 9:00 spike for JavaScript, CSS and images never reaches the servers.

3. **Stateless app servers behind a load balancer**, with autoscaling scheduled up before 9:00 instead of reacting after the spike hits.

4. **Cache the quiz questions.** Every student reads the same quiz, so it can be served from cache almost entirely.

5. **Queue the answer submissions.** Accept each submission quickly, write it to a queue, and let workers save and grade it at a steady rate, so a write burst cannot overwhelm the database.

6. **Add a read replica** for reports and dashboards, so teachers checking results do not slow down students.

Keep the database as a single primary unless measurements prove writes still cannot keep up. Sharding is a last resort.

takeaways: Measure before scaling. Often one slow query or missing index is the real problem.
Stateless app servers behind a load balancer can grow and shrink freely.
Caches absorb repeated reads. Queues absorb slow work and traffic spikes.
Every new component solves one bottleneck and adds complexity, so add them only when needed.
